chapter: Technique, jam sessions, audiences and records
title: The White arranger who sold arrangements to the band
summary: A White arranger selling arrangements at the Ritz Ballroom in Oklahoma City sold the Blue Devils four standards written to fit the band.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: [END OF TAPE 3, SIDE 2]
He was a white guy who used to do arrangements for the Blue Devils, and I think he wrote for Paul Whiteman.
Yeah.
Can you remember his name?
No, I can't remember his name now.
Buster Smith - 114
It wasn't Bill Chase, was it?
No.
There was a guy called Ferde Grofe, Ferdinand Grofe...
No, it wasn't him.
How did you come across him?

He happened to be passing through Oklahoma City. We was workin' at the Ritz Ballroom there, the Blue Devils. All the arrangers would do that. They'd come down to where the band was playing and ask you if you wanted to buy some arrangements and things like that. He was selling arrangements for ten dollars apiece, and we bought four. It was all standard numbers.
Were they good?
Yeah, they were good ones. He wrote it all in ink where it wouldn't blur any, and it wouldn't spoil, you couldn't rub it out...
I mean, would he have to adapt the arrangements according to the instrumentation of the band he was selling to?
No.
I mean, it's no good writing three trumpet parts if there's only two trumpet parts in the band. What did he do about that?
Yeah. He'd write for all of them. He came down to see the instrumentation of the band.
You mean, he'd come and hear the band first.
Yeah!
Buster Smith - 115
And then write it.
Yeah!
I see.
Yeah, he'd come down and see how many instruments you got, and what you got there, tenor or C-melody or what it is...
I see.
Yeah, all of them. He'd just write to fit the band.
I didn't know that White arrangers went around that for Black bands.
Yeah.
There were a lot of them doing that.
